claims.text: WTaTiVZr is an equimolar alloy containing approximately 20 at.% each of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr.
The alloying elements in WTaTiVZr are refractory and relatively low-activation.
Introducing Ta, Ti, V, and Zr into W promotes microstructural refinement.
The multicomponent alloy composition promotes formation of nanoscale second-phase precipitates.
The proposed nanoscale precipitates occur at grain boundaries and within grains.
The proposed second phases are likely rich in Ti- and Zr-containing compounds.
The nanoscale precipitates act as dispersion-strengthening obstacles.
The proposed precipitates impede or arrest crack propagation.
The proposed precipitates facilitate controlled dislocation motion.
The precipitate-containing microstructure promotes energy dissipation during plastic deformation.
Commercially used pure tungsten has a relatively homogeneous microstructure compared with the proposed WTaTiVZr microstructure.
Pure tungsten tends to be more brittle under high-temperature conditions than the WTaTiVZr alloy is predicted to be.
Under otherwise identical testing at 1500–2000 °C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater plastic strain before failure than pure tungsten.
Under otherwise identical testing at 1500–2000 °C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit higher fracture toughness than pure tungsten.
Comparable initial grain sizes and minimal prior deformation are proposed for the alloy and pure-tungsten specimens.
Pure tungsten tested with the same temperature, atmosphere, strain rate, and thermal history is proposed as the control.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply under high-temperature, high-strain-rate plasma-facing-component service conditions.
Applicability of the mechanism at lower temperatures or substantially different loading conditions is uncertain.
